ieltsReading.title: Learning in the garden
ieltsReading.text: When the primary school in a small town near the river opened its garden five years ago, many parents were doubtful. The head teacher, Ms Sophea, wanted children to learn science and maths by growing vegetables, but some families worried that it would take time away from reading and writing. Today, the garden covers about half of the school's land. Each class looks after its own section, and pupils measure how fast the plants grow, record the weather and calculate how much they can sell at the weekly market. The money pays for books and for school trips. According to the school's own records, pupils' maths results have improved every year since the garden began, although Ms Sophea admits that a new maths teacher, who joined at the same time, may also have made a difference. Not every school could copy the idea: the garden needs water all year, and in the dry season older pupils carry it from a well. Several schools in the province have visited, and two have started small gardens of their own.

statements.text: Some parents were not sure about the garden at first.
statements.why: "Many parents were doubtful."

statements.text: The garden is bigger than the school buildings.
statements.why: It covers half of the land; the buildings' size is never given.

statements.text: Every class grows the same vegetables.
statements.why: Each class has its own section, but the text does not say what they grow.

statements.text: Money from the market is spent on books.
statements.why: "The money pays for books and for school trips."

statements.text: Ms Sophea thinks the garden is the only reason maths results improved.
statements.why: She admits the new maths teacher may also have made a difference.

statements.text: In the dry season the garden's water comes from the river.
statements.why: Older pupils carry it from a well.

ieltsReading.title: Why we forget new words
ieltsReading.text: In the 1880s, the German researcher Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory by learning lists of nonsense syllables and checking how many he could remember after different amounts of time. He found that most forgetting happens soon after learning: a lot is lost within the first day, and after that it is lost more slowly. He also found that reviewing material several times, with gaps between the reviews, made it last much longer than studying it many times in one sitting. Modern researchers call this the spacing effect, and many studies since then have confirmed it. Some language-learning apps now use it to decide when to show each word again. However, scientists point out that memory also depends on other things, such as sleep, interest in the subject and whether a word is used in real conversation. A word that you say to a friend may be remembered better than one you only read on a screen.

statements.text: Ebbinghaus tested his ideas on other people.
statements.why: He tested his own memory.

statements.text: Forgetting is fastest soon after learning.
statements.why: "Most forgetting happens soon after learning."

statements.text: Other scientists of his time did not accept Ebbinghaus's work.
statements.why: The text says nothing about how scientists of his time reacted.

statements.text: Studying something many times in one session works better than spaced reviews.
statements.why: Spaced reviews made it last much longer.

statements.text: Sleep can affect how well we remember.
statements.why: Memory "also depends on other things, such as sleep".

statements.text: Most language-learning apps use the spacing effect.
statements.why: It says "some" apps use it; it does not say how many.

ieltsReading.title: The night market
ieltsReading.text: Every Friday and Saturday evening, the car park behind the town's main bus station becomes a night market. It started three years ago with about twenty food stalls, and it now has more than eighty, selling clothes, phone accessories and handmade jewellery as well as food. The market is run by a group of local sellers rather than by the town council, and each stall pays a small fee to cover cleaning and electricity. Most visitors are young people who come after work or college, but on Saturdays many families bring their children for the live music. The organisers say that the market has helped people who lost their jobs to start small businesses. Not everyone is happy, however. Some shop owners in the town centre complain that they have lost customers since the market opened, and people living nearby have asked for the music to end earlier. The organisers have agreed to stop the music at ten o'clock, but they say they have no plans to open on weekdays.

statements.text: The market takes place in a car park.
statements.why: "The car park behind the town's main bus station becomes a night market."

statements.text: The town council runs the market.
statements.why: It is run by local sellers "rather than by the town council".

statements.text: The stall fee has gone up since the market opened.
statements.why: The fee is mentioned, but not whether it has changed.

statements.text: Families mostly come on Saturdays.
statements.why: "On Saturdays many families bring their children."

statements.text: Some shop owners are unhappy about the market.
statements.why: They "complain that they have lost customers".

statements.text: The market will soon open on weekdays too.
statements.why: They "have no plans to open on weekdays".

ieltsReading.title: Bicycles made of bamboo
ieltsReading.text: In a small workshop outside a city, a group of young people builds bicycle frames from bamboo. The project began four years ago, when an engineering student noticed how much bamboo grew around her village and wondered whether it could replace steel. Bamboo is light and strong, and it absorbs the shock of bumpy roads, which makes riding more comfortable. Each frame takes about two weeks to make by hand, and the team now sells around thirty bicycles a month, mostly to customers abroad. The bicycles cost more than ordinary ones, but buyers say they last well if they are kept dry. The founder hopes to open a training centre so that other villages can start similar workshops. However, she admits that finding reliable glue, which has to be imported, has been a constant problem.

statements.text: The project was started by an engineering student.
statements.why: "An engineering student noticed how much bamboo grew around her village."

statements.text: Bamboo makes riding on bumpy roads less comfortable.
statements.why: It absorbs the shock, "which makes riding more comfortable".

statements.text: Most of the bicycles are sold to customers in other countries.
statements.why: They are sold "mostly to customers abroad".

statements.text: The team makes about thirty frames a week.
statements.why: About thirty bicycles a month; each frame takes about two weeks.

statements.text: The bamboo bicycles are cheaper than ordinary ones.
statements.why: "The bicycles cost more than ordinary ones."

statements.text: The glue the team uses comes from Japan.
statements.why: The glue is imported, but the text does not say from where.

ieltsReading.title: Sleep and learning
ieltsReading.text: Many students stay up late before exams, but research suggests that this may be a mistake. During sleep, the brain appears to replay and strengthen what was learned during the day. In one well-known type of experiment, people learn a list of words or a simple task, and then either sleep or stay awake for several hours before they are tested. Those who sleep usually remember more. Short naps can also help, although they seem to be most useful when they last less than an hour. Scientists are less certain about how much sleep different people need: most adults need between seven and nine hours, but the right amount varies. Caffeine late in the day can reduce the quality of sleep, even for people who say they sleep well after coffee.

statements.text: Staying up late before an exam is always a good idea.
statements.why: Research suggests "this may be a mistake".

statements.text: In these experiments, people who slept usually remembered more.
statements.why: "Those who sleep usually remember more."

statements.text: Naps longer than two hours help memory most.
statements.why: Naps seem most useful when they last less than an hour.

statements.text: Scientists know exactly how much sleep each person needs.
statements.why: Scientists are "less certain"; the right amount varies.

statements.text: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep.
statements.why: "Most adults need between seven and nine hours."

statements.text: Coffee affects children's sleep more than adults' sleep.
statements.why: Children are not mentioned.

ieltsReading.title: Schools on the water
ieltsReading.text: In some parts of the world, floods make it impossible for children to reach school for weeks every year. One solution has been the floating school: a boat that collects children from riverside villages and holds lessons on board. The idea was first tried by a local charity in a river delta, and it has since been copied in several other countries. A typical floating school has one classroom, a small library and solar panels that power lights and a few laptops. Teachers say that attendance has improved, especially among girls, whose families had worried about long journeys on foot. However, the boats are expensive to maintain, and most depend on donations. Some governments have started to pay part of the costs.

statements.text: Floods can stop children from getting to school.
statements.why: Floods "make it impossible for children to reach school".

statements.text: A government built the first floating school.
statements.why: It was "first tried by a local charity".

statements.text: Floating schools use solar power.
statements.why: They have "solar panels that power lights and a few laptops".

statements.text: Each floating school has several classrooms.
statements.why: A typical one "has one classroom".

statements.text: Fewer boys go to school since the floating schools began.
statements.why: The text says girls' attendance improved; it says nothing about boys falling.

statements.text: All floating schools are now paid for by governments.
statements.why: Most depend on donations; some governments pay part.

ieltsListening.title: Booking a homestay
ieltsListening.intro: A woman phones a homestay to book a room. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good morning, Green River Homestay. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Hello. I'd like to book a room for my husband and me, please.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Of course. Can I have your name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's Sreymom. That's S, R, E, Y, M, O, M.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you. And when would you like to come?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: We'd like to arrive on the fourteenth of April and stay for three nights.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's fine. A double room is twenty-five dollars a night, with breakfast.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Great. Can you also book us a boat trip?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. The boat trip leaves at seven thirty in the morning. Can I take a phone number?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Sure. It's oh one two, four five eight, nine oh three.

ieltsListening.title: Renting a flat
ieltsListening.intro: A man phones about a flat to rent. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Hello, City Homes. How can I help?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'm calling about the flat on Street sixty-three.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Ah yes, the two-bedroom flat. It's on the fourth floor.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is there a lift?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, there is. The rent is three hundred and fifty dollars a month.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Does that include water?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Water, yes, but not electricity.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: When can I see it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: How about Thursday at ten in the morning?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Perfect. My family name is Kim. That's K, I, M.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you, Mr Kim. Please bring your passport.

ieltsListening.title: Joining a gym
ieltsListening.intro: A woman joins a gym. Complete the form.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Welcome to FitLife. Are you interested in joining?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. What kinds of membership do you have?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Monthly is forty dollars, or you can pay four hundred for a whole year.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I'll take the yearly one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Great. Can I have your full name?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Sophea Long. Long is L, O, N, G.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And your date of birth?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The second of September, nineteen ninety-eight.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Do you have any health problems we should know about?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Only a bad back, from an old injury.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: OK, we'll tell your trainer. Your first session is on Monday at six thirty in the evening.
